lesson.title: A Few Pioneers, a Whole New Gene Pool: The Founder Effect
lesson.summary: The founder effect is a special case of genetic drift that occurs when a new population is established by a small number of individuals whose alleles, purely by chance, do not represent the full genetic variation of the source population they came from.
lesson.body:
The founder effect describes what happens when a new population is started by a small number of individuals who become isolated from their larger source population, whether by colonizing a remote island, crossing a mountain range, or being carried to a new habitat by wind, water, or human transport. Because genetic drift is strongest in small populations, and a founding group is about as small as a population gets, whatever alleles those few founders happen to carry, and in whatever frequencies they happen to carry them, become the entire genetic starting point for everything that follows. If an allele was rare in the source population, the founders might carry none of it at all, so it never appears in the new population. If an allele was uncommon but one of the founders happened to carry it, it can end up disproportionately common among their descendants, again for no adaptive reason whatsoever.

Consider a small group of finches blown off course during a storm and landing on a previously uninhabited island. Whatever variation existed among plumage color genes, beak shape genes, or any other trait back in the mainland population, only a fraction of it made the trip in these few birds. Their descendants carry that reduced, skewed sample forward, generation after generation, even after the island population eventually grows large. Human populations show the same pattern: several human communities that trace their ancestry back to a small number of founding settlers, isolated by geography, culture, or history, show measurably elevated frequencies of specific recessive genetic disorders. These disorders are not more common because the environment favored them. They are more common because one or more of the original founders happened, by chance, to carry the allele, and the population's small starting size meant that single chance event had an outsized and lasting effect on the entire gene pool.

The defining feature of the founder effect, and what distinguishes it from ordinary drift in an already established population, is the founding moment itself: a brand new population's entire genetic makeup is set by a tiny, non-random sample of a larger gene pool. The usual result is a new population with less overall genetic diversity than its source, along with allele frequencies that may look nothing like the source population's, purely because of who happened to be in the founding group. This matters for conservation biology and medicine alike. Island species and human populations founded by small groups are often more vulnerable to harmful recessive alleles simply reaching higher frequency, and less able to weather future environmental change because they carry less raw genetic variation to select from in the first place.
